The name of the Armenian goddess Anahit, used as a given name today. Written Անահիտ. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §778; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians V.25)

Used in early Armenia: Anoysh, first wife of the Median king Azhdahak, settled in Armenia by Tigran (legend); also the root of women's names like Sahakanush and Vardanush; an Iranian name. Written Անոյշ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.30)
Used in early Armenia: Bambish, sister of King Tiran and mother of Nerses the Great, 4th c.; a Middle Persian name. Written Բամբիշն. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.15, III.19, IV.3)

Used in early Armenia: Erato, queen of Armenia around the turn of the era, the last of her line; her portrait is on coins beside Tigran IV; a Greek name. Written Էրատո. (Tacitus, Annals 2.4; coin of Tigran IV and Erato, Artaxata, Bedoukian 128)
Used in early Armenia: Gayane, abbess of the Roman virgins martyred at Vagharshapat, c. 301 (traditional date); from Latin. Written Գայիանէ. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §138, 766)
Used in early Armenia: Mane, a companion of Hripsime who lived as a hermit in the Caves of Mane, 4th c.; of uncertain origin. Written Մանէ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.91)
Used in early Armenia: Mariam, wife of Gregory the Illuminator, who became a nun, late 3rd c.; from Hebrew. Written Մարիամ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.80)
The name of the Armenian goddess Nane, used as a given name today. Written Նանէ. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §786)

Used in early Armenia: Nazinik, a singer at the court of Bakur, lord of Aghdznik, in King Trdat's time (legend); of uncertain origin. Written Նազինիկ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.63)
Used in early Armenia: Nune (Saint Nino), a companion of Hripsime who converted the Iberians, 4th c.; of uncertain origin. Written Նունէ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.86)
Used in early Armenia: Nvard, beloved wife of Ara the Beautiful (legend); of uncertain origin. Written Նուարդ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.20)
Used in early Armenia: Satenik, the Alan princess who married King Artashes I, 2nd c. BCE (legend); of uncertain origin. Written Սաթենիկ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.49–50)

Used in early Armenia: Shamiram (Semiramis), the legendary Assyrian queen who loved Ara the Beautiful; a name of Armenian women since the 15th century; a Syriac name. Written Շամիրամ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.15–19)
from the Iranian word for gold, with the feminine ending -uhi
Used in early Armenia: Zaruhi, wife of the legendary king Tigran Yervandian; formed from Iranian 'gold' + Armenian feminine -uhi. Written Զարուհի. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.29)
Used in early Armenia: Amasia, legendary descendant of Hayk, son of Aramayis; of uncertain origin. Written Ամասիա. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.12)
Used in early Armenia: Ara the Beautiful, legendary king loved by Shamiram; an Armenian name. Written Արա. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.3, I.15)
Used in early Armenia: Aram, legendary patriarch after whom, Khorenatsi says, Armenia was named; an Armenian name. Written Արամ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.3, I.13–14)
The name of the Armenian god Aramazd, used as a given name today. Written Արամազդ. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §786)
Used in early Armenia: the blessed Arsen, priest martyred in the Persian captivity, 5th c.; from Greek. Written Արսէն. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §39)
Used in early Armenia: Arshak II, king of Armenia, r. c. 350–368; a Parthian name. Written Արշակ. (Ammianus Marcellinus 20.11.1–3, 'Arsaces'; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.1)
Used in early Armenia: Arsham, king of Armenia in Khorenatsi's account of the Parthian era; an Old Persian name. Written Արշամ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.24)
a pet form of names built on 'truth'
Used in early Armenia: Artak, lord of Mokk, at the council of 450; a Middle Iranian name. Written Արտակ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23)
Used in early Armenia: Ashot, aspet of the Bagratunis, father of Pap Bagratuni, late 6th c.; of uncertain origin. Written Աշոտ. (Sebeos, History ch. 11)

Used in early Armenia: Atom Gnuni, lord of Gnunik, at the council of 450; of uncertain origin. Written Ատոմ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.12)
Used in early Armenia: Babken Syuni, brother of Bakur, in Vahan Mamikonian's revolt, 480s; of uncertain origin. Written Բաբգէն. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §47)
Used in early Armenia: Bagarat, great prince of the aspetutiwn, 4th c.; an Iranian name. Written Բագարատ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.21)
Used in early Armenia: Daniel, Syrian-born bishop in Taron, killed by King Tiran, 4th c.; from Hebrew. Written Դանիէլ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.14)
Used in early Armenia: Davit, priest at the council of 450; from Syriac. Written Դաւիթ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23)
Used in early Armenia: Gagik Mamikonian, son of Manuel, late 6th c.; of uncertain origin. Written Գագիկ. (Sebeos, History ch. 11)
Used in early Armenia: Garegin, lord of Rshtunik, husband of Hamazaspuhi, 4th c.; an Armenian name. Written Գարեգին. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.59, V.37)
Used in early Armenia: Gegham, legendary descendant of Hayk who settled by Lake Sevan; of uncertain origin. Written Գեղամ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.12)

Used in early Armenia: Gnel, nephew of King Arshak II, killed on his orders, c. 359; of uncertain origin. Written Գնէլ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.21, IV.15; Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part One §15)
Used in early Armenia: Gregory the Illuminator, who converted Armenia, d. c. 331; from Greek. Written Գրիգոր. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.2)
Used in early Armenia: Hayk, legendary forefather of the Armenians, who defeated Bel; an Armenian name. Written Հայկ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.10–12)
Used in early Armenia: Hovhan Mandakuni, catholicos of Armenia, 478–490; from Hebrew. Written Յովհան. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Three §70)
Used in early Armenia: Hovsep of Paghanakan, pupil of Mashtots and later catholicos, d. 454; from Hebrew. Written Յովսէփ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part One §10)
Used in early Armenia: Hrant, legendary king in Khorenatsi's list of Hayk's descendants; of uncertain origin. Written Հրանտ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.19)
Used in early Armenia: Yusik, catholicos of Armenia, grandson of Gregory, killed by King Tiran, 4th c.; an Armenian name. Written Յուսիկ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.12)
Used in early Armenia: Manuel Mamikonian, commander of Armenia, d. c. 385; from Hebrew. Written Մանուէլ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians V.37, V.44)

Used in early Armenia: Mesrop Mashtots, inventor of the Armenian alphabet, d. 440; of uncertain origin. Written Մեսրոպ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part One §10; Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians III.47)
The name of the Armenian god Mihr, also an early Armenian man's name. Written Միհր. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §790)
Used in early Armenia: Movses, catholicos in the Persian part of Armenia, late 6th c.; from Hebrew. Written Մովսէս. (Sebeos, History ch. 9)
Used in early Armenia: Nerses the Great, catholicos of Armenia, d. 373; a Middle Persian name. Written Ներսէս. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.3)
Used in early Armenia: Norayr, legendary king in Khorenatsi's list of Hayk's descendants; of uncertain origin. Written Նորայր. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.19)

Used in early Armenia: Pap, king of Armenia, r. 370–374, son of Arshak II and Parandzem; a Middle Iranian name. Written Պապ. (Ammianus Marcellinus 27.12.9, 'Papa'; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians V.1)
Used in early Armenia: Paruyr son of Skayordi, legendary first crowned king of the Armenians; of uncertain origin. Written Պարոյր. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.21–22)

Used in early Armenia: Sahak the Great, catholicos, patron of the Armenian alphabet, d. 439; from Hebrew. Written Սահակ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part One §10; Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians III.49)
Used in early Armenia: Sargis, a Vahevuni lord who rebelled in the Byzantine sector, late 6th c.; from Syriac. Written Սարգիս. (Sebeos, History ch. 7)
Used in early Armenia: Shavarsh, legendary king in Khorenatsi's list of Hayk's descendants; a Middle Iranian name. Written Շաւարշ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.19)
Used in early Armenia: Sisak, son of Gegham, legendary ancestor of the lords of Syunik; of uncertain origin. Written Սիսակ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.12)
Used in early Armenia: Smbat Bagratuni, Armenian prince and general, c. 600; an Iranian name. Written Սմբատ. (Sebeos, History ch. 10)

Used in early Armenia: Tigran II the Great, king of Armenia, r. 95–55 BCE; the name is on the coins of Tigran IV; an Iranian name. Written Տիգրան. (Plutarch, Life of Lucullus 21; coin of Tigran IV with legend ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΜΕΓΑΣ ΤΙΓΡΑΝΗΣ)
The name of the Armenian god Tir. Written Տիր. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §778)
Used in early Armenia: Tiran, king of Armenia, r. c. 339–350; an Iranian name. Written Տիրան. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.12)
Used in early Armenia: Vache Mamikonian, commander of Armenia, killed fighting the Persians, c. 336; of uncertain origin. Written Վաչէ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.11)

The name of the Armenian god Vahagn, used as a given name today. Written Վահագն. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §809; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.14; Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.31)
Used in early Armenia: Vahan Mamikonian, leader of the revolt of 481–484 and marzpan of Armenia; of uncertain origin. Written Վահան. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Three §63)
Used in early Armenia: Vahe, last legendary Haykazun king, who rose against Alexander; an Iranian name. Written Վահէ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.31)
Used in early Armenia: Vardan Mamikonian, commander of Armenia, killed at Avarayr in 451; an Iranian name. Written Վարդան. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23, §30)
from an Iranian word for 'ruling at will, sovereign'
Used in early Armenia: Vasak Mamikonian, commander of Armenia, d. c. 367; an Iranian name. Written Վասակ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.16)
Used in early Armenia: Zareh, prince of Greater Tsopk, 4th c.; an Iranian name. Written Զարեհ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.12)
Used in early Armenia: Zarmayr, legendary king said to have fought at Troy; of uncertain origin. Written Զարմայր. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.19, I.31a)
Used in early Armenia: Zaven, bishop of Mananaghi, at the council of 450; an Iranian name. Written Զաւէն. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23)
Used in early Armenia: Ashkhen, queen of King Trdat III, who helped build the martyrs' chapels, early 4th c.; a Middle Iranian name. Written Աշխէն. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §766, 791)
The name of the Armenian goddess Astghik, used as a given name today. Written Աստղիկ. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §809)
probably 'cast away', a name for a foundling

Used in early Armenia: Hripsime, Roman virgin martyred at Vagharshapat, c. 301 (traditional date); from Greek. Written Հռիփսիմէ. (Agathangelos, History of the Armenians §138; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.14)

Used in early Armenia: Olympias, Roman noblewoman married to King Arshak II, poisoned c. 361; a Greek name. Written Ողոմպի. (Ammianus Marcellinus 20.11.3; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.15)
its first part means 'glory'; the second is disputed
Used in early Armenia: Parandzem, queen of Arshak II and mother of King Pap, d. c. 370; a Parthian name. Written Փառանձեմ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.15, IV.54)

Used in early Armenia: Sahakanush, daughter of Catholicos Sahak the Great, wife of Hamazasp Mamikonian and mother of Vardan, 5th c.; formed from Hebrew Sahak + Iranian anoyš. Written Սահականոյշ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians III.51)

Used in early Armenia: Sandukht, daughter of King Sanatruk, martyred with the apostle Thaddeus (tradition); a Middle Persian name. Written Սանդուխտ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.34)

Used in early Armenia: Shushanik, daughter of Vardan Mamikonian, queen in Iberia, martyred c. 475; formed from Armenian Shushan 'lily' + diminutive -ik. Written Շուշանիկ. (Iakob Tsurtaveli, Martyrdom of Shushanik, 5th c., in Georgian)

Used in early Armenia: Tigranuhi, sister of the legendary king Tigran Yervandian, given in marriage to the Median king Azhdahak; formed from Iranian Tigran + Armenian feminine -uhi. Written Տիգրանուհի. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.24, I.28, I.30)
Used in early Armenia: Vardanush, wife of the commander Manuel Mamikonian, late 4th c.; formed from Iranian Vardan + anoyš. Written Վարդանոյշ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians V.43)

Used in early Armenia: Anushavan Sawsanver, legendary son of Ara son of Ara; the name was revived in the 19th century; of uncertain origin. Written Անուշաւան. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.19–20)
one who strives for peace and joy
Used in early Armenia: Aramayis, legendary son of Aramaneak and founder of Armavir; a Middle Iranian name. Written Արամայիս. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.3, I.12)
Used in early Armenia: Aristakes, son of Gregory the Illuminator, catholicos, at the Council of Nicaea, 325; from Greek. Written Արիստակէս. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.2)
Used in early Armenia: Aramaneak, son of Hayk; Armenak is the modern form, revived in the 18th century; an Armenian name. Written Արմենակ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.3, I.12)
Used in early Armenia: Arshavir Kamsarakan, prince of Shirak and Arsharunik, 4th c.; an Iranian name. Written Արշաւիր. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.11)
Used in early Armenia: Artashes I (Artaxias), founder of the Artaxiad kingdom, early 2nd c. BCE; a Southwestern Iranian name. Written Արտաշէս. (Strabo, Geography 11.14.5, 11.14.15)
Used in early Armenia: Ghazar Parpetsi, historian of Armenia, c. 500; from Hebrew. Written Ղազար. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians, the author himself)
Used in early Armenia: Grigoris, grandson of Gregory, bishop among the Albanians, martyred 4th c.; from Greek. Written Գրիգորիս. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.5–6)
Used in early Armenia: Hamazasp Mamikonian, commander of Armenia, father of Vardan, early 5th c.; an Iranian name. Written Համազասպ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part One §18)
Used in early Armenia: Hmayak Mamikonian, brother of Vardan, killed in 451; an Iranian name. Written Հմայեակ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part One §18)
Used in early Armenia: Hrachya, legendary king 'so named because of his very radiant face and fiery eyes'; an Armenian name. Written Հրաչեայ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians I.22)
Used in early Armenia: Hrahat, lord of Ashotsk, at the council of 450; an Iranian name. Written Հրահատ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23)
Used in early Armenia: Khad, bishop of Bagrevand, deputy of Nerses the Great, 4th c.; an Armenian name. Written Խադ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians IV.12)
Used in early Armenia: Khosrov Kotak, king of Armenia, r. c. 330–339, son of Trdat; a Middle Iranian name. Written Խոսրով. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.3, III.11)
Used in early Armenia: Mushegh Mamikonian, commander of Armenia, killed c. 378; a Hittite name. Written Մուշեղ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians V.2)

Used in early Armenia: Sanatruk, king of Armenia remembered as the killer of the apostle Thaddeus, 1st c. (tradition); a Parthian name. Written Սանատրուկ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.34–36; Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.1)
Used in early Armenia: Tachat Rshtuni, son of Mehendak, saved as an infant in a 4th-c. massacre; of uncertain origin. Written Տաճատ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.18)
Used in early Armenia: Vagharsh, prince of Anjit and great hazarapet of Armenia, 4th c.; a Parthian name. Written Վաղարշ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians III.12)
Used in early Armenia: Varazdat, king of Armenia, r. 374–378; a Middle Persian name. Written Վարազդատ. (Pʿawstos Buzand, History of the Armenians V.34–37)
Used in early Armenia: Yeghishe, bishop of Amatunik, at the council of 450; from Syriac. Written Եղիշէ. (Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians Part Two §23)
Used in early Armenia: Yervand, last king of the Orontid line, overthrown by Artashes, c. 200 BCE; a Middle Iranian name. Written Երուանդ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians II.37–46)
Used in early Armenia: Yeznik of Koghb, translator and theologian, pupil of Mashtots, 5th c.; an Armenian name. Written Եզնիկ. (Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians III.60)
